newsitem.title: USA: Big risks seen in bank-commerce mix -- US GAO report.
newsitem.headline: Big risks seen in bank-commerce mix -- US GAO report.

text.p: Allowing banks to combine with commercial companies as contemplated under some recently introduced bank reform legislation could jeopardize the U.S. financial system, according to a Congressional research report released on Thursday.

"Eliminating the separation of banking and commerce might subject the financial system, the deposit insurance fund, and consumers and taxpayers to a variety of risks," the General Accounting Office said in its report. "Potential benefits generally lacked empirical support and ... could be realized without having to remove the barriers."

House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, a vocal opponent of allowing banks and nonfinancial firms to mix, said the study cast doubt on financial service reform proposals that would permit unlimited combinations.

"As the study emphasizes, Congress should move judiciously and with the greatest caution in enacting any changes to the separation of commerce and banking, so that taxpayer money and the American economy not be put in jeopardy," the Iowa Republican said.
Leach has introduced a bill that would allow banks to combine with financial firms, but generally not others.
By contrast, a bill introduced by Rep Richard Baker, Republican of Lousiania, would impose no limits on banking and commerce.

Rep Marge Roukema, Republican of New Jersey, and Rep Bruce Vento, Democrat from Minnesota, would allow financial firms to conduct up to 25 percent of their business in nonfinancial activities, often referred to as a "basket" approach.
The Clinton administration is expected to release its own bank reform measure shortly.
The administration was initially seen leaning towards Baker's position.
But recently people familiar with the measure said the proposal would likely include a more limited basket approach.
The GAO report said allowing unlimited mixing could result in a concentration of economic power in a few huge conglomerates.

"Such enterprises could adversely affect the efficient operation of the economy and place consumers at risk of increased prices if they began to exert market power in either their banking or commercial operations," the report said.
Conglomerates could also expand the federal safety net which is designed to protect depositors if a bank fails.
If a firm's commercial operation failed, the federal government might have to step in to protect the firm's bank depositors, GAO said.

Conglomerates "would increase the risk that the safety net, and associated subsidy, might be transferred to commercial operations and result in inappropriate risk-taking, misallocations of resources, and uneven competitive playing fields in other industries," GAO said.

"While such risks might be mitigated by establishing firewalls between banks and their commercial affiliates, our work has shown that such firewalls may not work in times of stress, or where managers are determined to evade them," GAO added.
Proponents of mixing banking and commerce have argued that such firewalls would prevent a widening of the safety net.

And since insurance companies, securities firms and some thrifts are already involved in nonfinancial activity, they would be at a disadvantage relative to banks if they were forced to divest those holdings under financial reform, proponents said.
With Congress in recess, no one was immediately available to comment in the offices of Rep Baker and Rep Roukema.
--Aaron Pressman((202-8908-8312))
